subject: PHS
subtopic: Challenging patient and ethical scenarios: adherence, disclosure, minors
vignette: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus returns for follow-up. His hemoglobin A1c has risen from 7.2% to 9.4%, and his blood pressure is 148/92 mm Hg. He admits he has been skipping his metformin and lisinopril because of the cost and because he often cannot get a ride to the pharmacy. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Given the difficulty you have described, I will refer you to another physician who may be able to manage your diabetes more effectively.
Let's talk about the barriers that have kept you from taking your medications, and let's schedule regular follow-up visits so we can work through them together.
If you keep skipping your medications, you will go blind and end up on dialysis, so you need to start taking them every day.
Taking your medications is not a matter of choice; I need you to commit to the plan we agreed on.
Your diabetes is really not that bad, so missing some doses now and then is unlikely to make much of a difference.

explanation_correct: When a patient does not follow the medical plan, the physician should determine whether there are financial, logistical, or other obstacles preventing adherence — here, cost and lack of transportation. Coercing the patient, threatening him, or referring him to another physician is inappropriate. Scheduling regular follow-up visits to track progress and problem-solve barriers is the recommended approach.

explanation_incorrect.A: Referring a nonadherent patient to another physician is explicitly inappropriate; nonadherence is a problem to work through with the patient, not a reason to transfer care.
explanation_incorrect.C: This uses fear to pressure the patient into adhering, which is coercive; the correct approach is to identify and address the concrete obstacles, not to threaten him with complications.
explanation_incorrect.D: This is an authoritarian, coercive statement that ignores the financial and logistical barriers the patient has just disclosed and does not invite collaboration.
explanation_incorrect.E: This is falsely reassuring: the hemoglobin A1c rose from 7.2% to 9.4%, showing clear worsening, and minimizing missed doses dismisses a real barrier to care.

educationalObjective: For nonadherence, identify financial, logistical, or other obstacles and schedule regular follow-up; never coerce or refer the patient elsewhere.

subject: PHS
subtopic: Challenging patient and ethical scenarios: adherence, disclosure, minors
vignette: A 45-year-old woman presents for the third time this year asking you to order a brain MRI for her headaches. Her headaches are consistent with tension-type headaches, her neurologic examination is normal, and she has no red-flag features. She says, 'I just need to know it is not a tumor.' Which of the following is the most appropriate response?
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: I will order the MRI so that we can put this concern behind us once and for all.
You should find another physician, because I cannot care for someone who insists on tests that are not indicated.
An MRI is not indicated for your headaches, and I will not order one no matter how many times you ask.
Help me understand what worries you most about these headaches, and let's talk about what an MRI would and would not tell us.
I will refer you to a neurologist, since headaches like yours are beyond what I can manage in this office.

explanation_correct: When a patient desires an unnecessary procedure, the physician should attempt to understand why the patient wants it and address the underlying concerns — here, fear of a brain tumor. The physician should not refuse to see the patient or refer her elsewhere, and should avoid performing the unnecessary test. Exploring her worry and discussing what imaging would and would not show is patient-centered and respects autonomy.

explanation_incorrect.A: Ordering the MRI to end the argument performs an unnecessary procedure, which the physician should avoid even when the patient insists.
explanation_incorrect.B: Refusing to see the patient again because she requests testing is explicitly inappropriate; the physician must continue to address her underlying concerns.
explanation_incorrect.C: A flat, unconditional refusal does not explore why the patient wants the test or address her fear of cancer, and it closes off further discussion.
explanation_incorrect.E: Referring the patient elsewhere for a request the physician can and should address is inappropriate; the neurologist referral is a way of avoiding the conversation.

educationalObjective: For a patient requesting an unnecessary procedure, explore the motivation behind the request and address underlying concerns without performing the procedure, refusing care, or referring out.

subject: PHS
subtopic: Challenging patient and ethical scenarios: adherence, disclosure, minors
vignette: A 79-year-old woman with heart failure takes four daily medications. At a follow-up visit accompanied by her daughter, she admits she often skips doses because she cannot remember the instructions and finds the pill bottles confusing. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Let me give you written instructions in plain language, and then I would like you to explain back to me how and when you will take each medication.
Since you have managed these medications for years, I am confident you will remember them correctly from now on.
Forgetting doses at your age suggests worsening dementia, so I will refer you to a memory clinic for evaluation.
From now on your daughter must administer every dose, whether or not you agree to that arrangement.
Because the regimen is clearly too complicated for you, I am stopping two of your medications today without further discussion.

explanation_correct: When a patient has difficulty taking medications, the physician should determine what factors are involved. If comprehension or memory are issues, recommended techniques include providing written instructions, using the teach-back method (asking the patient to restate the plan in her own words), and simplifying the treatment regimen. Option A combines written instructions with teach-back, directly targeting her memory and comprehension difficulties.

explanation_incorrect.B: This is falsely reassuring and addresses nothing; the patient has just described an ongoing, concrete comprehension and memory problem that requires practical techniques.
explanation_incorrect.C: Skipping doses because of confusing instructions is a common medication-management issue, not evidence of worsening dementia, and an immediate referral avoids addressing the actual obstacle.
explanation_incorrect.D: Transferring all medication administration to the daughter without the patient's agreement is coercive and strips her of autonomy in managing her own care.
explanation_incorrect.E: Unilaterally stopping essential heart failure medications without discussion could harm the patient; simplifying a regimen should be a collaborative decision, not a silent unilateral act.

educationalObjective: For difficulty taking medications, identify contributing factors and use written instructions, teach-back, and regimen simplification when comprehension or memory is impaired.

subject: PHS
subtopic: Challenging patient and ethical scenarios: adherence, disclosure, minors
vignette: A 66-year-old man with metastatic pancreatic cancer is alert, oriented, and conversant. His wife and son stop you in the hallway and ask, 'How long does he have? Please tell us what to expect.' The patient has never discussed his prognosis with them, and you have not asked him whether he wants them to know. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: He has only a few months to live, so you should begin making the necessary arrangements.
I can share his prognosis with you as soon as your family completes the proper health information release forms.
I understand how difficult this uncertainty is; I would need his permission before discussing his prognosis with you, and I will encourage him to talk with you about it.
Let's step into the family room so we can talk about his prognosis without him hearing us.
You should ask him yourself; it would be inappropriate for me to say anything at all to you about his condition.

explanation_correct: Physicians should avoid discussing a patient's issues with relatives without the patient's permission. The competent patient owns the information about his own prognosis. The correct response validates the family's emotion, explains that the patient's permission is required, and encourages patient-family communication rather than disclosing or dodging outright.

explanation_incorrect.A: Disclosing a terminal prognosis to relatives without the patient's permission is a direct breach of confidentiality and violates his autonomy over his own health information.
explanation_incorrect.B: Paperwork does not resolve the core issue: the patient has not been asked whether he wants his prognosis shared, and his wishes — not administrative forms alone — should guide disclosure.
explanation_incorrect.D: Deliberately plotting to discuss the prognosis behind the alert patient's back is a confidentiality breach and is deceptive toward the patient.
explanation_incorrect.E: Although the confidentiality principle is right, this reply is cold and dismissive; it fails to acknowledge the family's distress and does not offer to facilitate communication.

educationalObjective: Do not discuss a patient's prognosis with relatives without the patient's permission; instead, empathize with the family and encourage the patient to share information himself.

subject: PHS
subtopic: Challenging patient and ethical scenarios: adherence, disclosure, minors
vignette: A 52-year-old woman was admitted for evaluation of a lung mass. Biopsy results show metastatic adenocarcinoma. Before you enter the room, her adult son stops you: 'In our family, the eldest son receives all medical news first. Please do not tell her the results — she will not be able to handle it.' The patient has been asking the nursing staff all morning when her results will be ready. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: I will respect your family's wishes and discuss the results with you first before she hears anything.
I will withhold the results for now, and we can revisit the decision if she asks me about them directly.
Because this diagnosis could cause her serious harm, I will invoke therapeutic privilege and withhold the results from her.
Your request is not my concern, so I will simply go in and tell her the results right now.
I appreciate your concern and your family's perspective; I will ask her how much she wants to know, and I will not withhold the information if she wants it.

explanation_correct: The physician should explore why the family member believes disclosure would be detrimental, including possible cultural factors — here, a family tradition of the eldest son receiving news first. If the patient would like information concerning her care, it must not be withheld. Therapeutic privilege (withholding information) is justified only if the physician believes the patient might seriously harm herself or others if informed, which is not suggested here. Asking the patient how much she wants to know respects her autonomy while honoring the family's cultural concern.

explanation_incorrect.A: Giving results to a relative first without the competent patient's consent violates her autonomy and her explicit requests to know her results.
explanation_incorrect.B: Withholding the diagnosis because the family fears she 'cannot handle it' is inappropriate when the patient herself is actively seeking the information and poses no danger to herself or others.
explanation_incorrect.C: This misuses therapeutic privilege: it applies only when the physician believes disclosure could lead to serious harm to the patient or others, not merely to anticipated emotional distress.
explanation_incorrect.D: Ignoring the son outright, although the disclosure position is correct, fails to explore the cultural reasons behind the request and is dismissive of the family's role.

educationalObjective: Explore cultural and emotional reasons when family asks to withhold bad news, never withhold information from a patient who wants it, and reserve therapeutic privilege for situations of potential serious harm.

subject: PHS
subtopic: Challenging patient and ethical scenarios: adherence, disclosure, minors
vignette: A 17-year-old woman at 8 weeks' gestation tells you she is pregnant and wants an abortion. In your state, parental notification is required for minors seeking abortion unless a judge grants a waiver. There are no medical complications of her pregnancy. She asks, 'What would you do in my situation?' Which of the following is the most appropriate response?
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: I would continue the pregnancy and make an adoption plan, since that is the safest path at your age.
This is your decision to make; let's discuss all of your options and the notification requirements in our state, and I will refer you for abortion care if that is what you choose.
Because you are a minor, I cannot discuss any of this with you until a parent is present in the room.
I would terminate the pregnancy, since continuing it would clearly interfere with your schooling.
Since there are no medical risks associated with your pregnancy, you should carry it to term and consider adoption afterward.

explanation_correct: Many states require parental notification or consent for minors seeking an abortion, and the physician should be familiar with these requirements. Unless there are specific medical risks associated with the pregnancy, the physician should not sway the patient's decision for or against an elective abortion, regardless of her age. The appropriate course is to discuss options for terminating the pregnancy and to refer for abortion care if needed, leaving the decision with the patient.

explanation_incorrect.A: Recommending continuation and adoption sways the patient's decision against abortion, which the physician should avoid when no specific medical risks are present.
explanation_incorrect.C: Refusing to counsel a minor about her pregnancy until a parent arrives is wrong; she may be counseled confidentially, and notification requirements pertain to the procedure, not to a discussion of options.
explanation_incorrect.D: Recommending abortion because of schooling sways the patient's decision in the opposite direction; the physician must not steer an elective abortion decision either for or against.
explanation_incorrect.E: Telling the patient what she 'should' do biases the decision against abortion; the physician's role is to lay out options neutrally, not to issue a directive.

educationalObjective: For a minor requesting abortion, know state notification laws, do not sway the decision absent specific medical risks, discuss all options, and refer for abortion care if desired.

subject: PHS
subtopic: Challenging patient and ethical scenarios: adherence, disclosure, minors
vignette: A 15-year-old patient is 20 weeks pregnant and tells you she plans to raise her baby. Her parents meet with you separately and demand that you tell her to place the child for adoption, insisting she is 'far too young to raise a baby.' Which of the following is the most appropriate response?
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Because you are a minor, your parents have the legal authority to decide what happens with the baby.
Your parents are right that raising a child at 15 is unrealistic, and adoption would give the baby a better life.
You have the right to make decisions about your child; let me give you practical information about caring for a baby, and I will encourage you and your parents to keep discussing this together.
I will tell your parents that you have agreed to adoption so that they stop pressuring you about it.
This decision is entirely between you and the baby's father, and your parents' opinions should not enter into it at all.

explanation_correct: The pregnant minor retains the right to make decisions regarding her child, even if her parents disagree. The physician should provide information about the practical aspects of caring for a baby, discuss options for terminating the pregnancy if requested, and encourage discussion between the patient and her parents to reach the best decision — all of which option C does.

explanation_incorrect.A: Parents do not hold decision-making authority over a pregnant minor's choices regarding her own child; the minor patient retains that right.
explanation_incorrect.B: Siding with the parents and endorsing adoption sways the patient's autonomous decision instead of supporting it with practical information.
explanation_incorrect.D: Telling the parents the patient agreed to adoption when she has not is deceptive and would betray the patient's confidence.
explanation_incorrect.E: Excluding the parents entirely contradicts the recommended approach of encouraging discussion between the patient and her parents to reach the best decision.

educationalObjective: A pregnant minor retains decision-making rights regarding her child; provide practical information and encourage patient-parent discussion rather than deferring to the parents.
